items.stem: What is meant by market failure?
options: A situation where a firm goes out of business
A situation where the free market leads to a misallocation of resources
A fall in the stock market
items.answer: A situation where the free market leads to a misallocation of resources
items.markingKey: Market fails to achieve an efficient (socially optimal) outcome.

items.stem: Explain what is meant by market failure and give two examples.
items.answer: Market failure is when the free market misallocates resources, so output is not at the socially optimal level. Examples: public goods not provided, negative externalities (pollution) over-produced, merit goods under-consumed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: definition; 1 mark each example [3]

items.stem: Explain why positive externalities lead to under-consumption in a free market.
items.answer: Consumers consider only their private benefit; the external benefit to others is ignored, so demand and consumption are below the socially optimal level.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: private benefit only; 1 mark: below social optimum [2]

items.stem: Smokers in Esteria underestimate the risk of lung disease. Which type of market failure is illustrated?
items.answer: Demerit good (information failure)
items.markingKey: Demerit good (information failure): harm is underestimated, so the good is over-consumed.

items.stem: One firm controls the entire water supply in Muscat and raises its prices. Which type of market failure is illustrated? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Monopoly power: lack of competition leads to high prices and lower output.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Monopoly power; 1 mark: explanation – lack of competition leads to high prices and lower output. [2]

items.stem: Extract: In Umbria Nova, childhood vaccination rates were only 60% when parents had to pay about $40 per course. After the government made vaccinations free and ran an information campaign, the rate rose to 82%. The health ministry argues that vaccination is a merit good with large external benefits. A newspaper claims that “the market would have sorted this out on its own”. (a) Explain why vaccination is a merit good. (b) Explain the external benefits of vaccination.
items.answer: (a) Parents underestimate the benefits (information failure), so it is under-consumed in a free market. (b) Vaccinated children protect others (herd immunity), lowering infection and healthcare costs for third parties.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Parents underestimate the benefits (information failure), so it is under-consumed in a free market. [2] (b) Credit: Vaccinated children protect others (herd immunity), lowering infection and healthcare costs for third parties. [2]

items.stem: Which is an example of market failure?
options: A fall in the price of a good after a rise in supply
Consumers switching to a cheaper brand
items.answer: The under-provision of public goods
items.markingKey: Missing markets, externalities, information failure, merit/demerit goods.

items.stem: Explain why monopoly power may be a reason for government intervention.
items.answer: A monopolist can restrict output and raise price above the competitive level, reducing consumer welfare and misallocating resources.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: higher price/lower output; 1 mark: misallocation [2]

items.stem: Traffic congestion in Auckland imposes costs on bus passengers and local residents. Explain why this is a market failure.
items.answer: Each driver ignores the extra delay and pollution they impose on others (negative externality), so road use exceeds the socially optimal level.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: external cost; 1 mark: over-use [2]

items.stem: Meridian Group researches a new vaccine that other firms can copy. Explain why the market may provide too little research.
items.answer: Research creates positive externalities (benefits to other firms and society) that Meridian Group cannot charge for, so it invests less than the social optimum.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: external benefits; 1 mark: under-investment [2]

items.stem: Redwood Corp produces 5,000 tonnes of chemicals a month. Its private cost is $10 per tonne, but pollution imposes an extra cost of $4 per tonne on local residents. Calculate the social cost per tonne.
items.markingKey: Social cost = private + external = 10 + 4.

items.stem: Identify the type of market failure in each case and explain why it leads to a misallocation of resources. (i) Beekeepers in Westaria help nearby farmers by pollinating their crops for free. (ii) Second-hand car buyers in Westaria cannot tell which cars are faulty, but sellers can.
items.answer: (i) Positive externality (ii) Asymmetric information
items.markingKey: (i) Positive externality – a benefit is received by third parties without payment. [2] (ii) Asymmetric information – one party has more information than the other. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: The government of Umbria Nova has asked its economic advisers for a report on this issue. Explain the main types of market failure that may justify government intervention.
items.answer: Public goods (free riders), externalities, merit and demerit goods, information failure, monopoly power; misallocation vs social optimum.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Public goods (free riders), externalities, merit and demerit goods, information failure, monopoly power; misallocation vs social optimum. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: What is asymmetric information?
options: A shortage of data for government
A situation where both parties have full information
A situation where one party to a transaction has more information than the other
items.answer: A situation where one party to a transaction has more information than the other
items.markingKey: e.g. sellers of used cars, insurance.

items.stem: Explain how information failure can lead to a misallocation of resources.
items.answer: If consumers misjudge the benefits or costs of a good, they buy too much (demerit) or too little (merit) compared with what they would buy with full information, so output is not at the social optimum.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: misjudge benefits/costs; 1 mark: wrong quantity vs optimum [2]

items.stem: Explain the case for the government providing education free at the point of use.
items.answer: Education is a merit good: families underestimate its benefits and there are positive externalities; some cannot afford it. Free provision raises consumption towards the social optimum and improves equity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: merit good/info failure; 1 mark: externalities; 1 mark: equity [3]

items.stem: Beekeepers in Calvania help nearby farmers by pollinating their crops for free. Which type of market failure is illustrated?
items.answer: Positive externality
items.markingKey: Positive externality: a benefit is received by third parties without payment.

items.stem: Street lighting in Jakarta would not be supplied by any private firm. Which type of market failure is illustrated? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Public good (free rider problem): non-excludable and non-rivalrous.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Public good (free rider problem); 1 mark: explanation – non-excludable and non-rivalrous. [2]

items.stem: Extract: In Umbria Nova, childhood vaccination rates were only 48% when parents had to pay about $50 per course. After the government made vaccinations free and ran an information campaign, the rate rose to 70%. The health ministry argues that vaccination is a merit good with large external benefits. A newspaper claims that “the market would have sorted this out on its own”. (a) Calculate the increase in the vaccination rate in percentage points. (b) Explain why the market alone might fail to achieve the socially optimal rate.
items.answer: (a) 22 percentage points (b) Consumers ignore external benefits and underestimate private benefits; price deters low-income families.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 22 percentage points [1] (b) Credit: Consumers ignore external benefits and underestimate private benefits; price deters low-income families. [3]

items.stem: The government of Halvoria pays for free health check-ups for adults over 50. Explain why.
items.answer: People underestimate the benefits of early diagnosis (information failure); early treatment is cheaper and has external benefits; check-ups are a merit good.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: info failure; 1 mark: benefits of provision [2]

items.answer: People underestimate the benefits of early diagnosis (information failure); early treatment is cheaper and has external benefits; check-ups are a merit good.

items.answer: Monopoly power
items.markingKey: Monopoly power: lack of competition leads to high prices and lower output.

items.stem: In Selmaria, 40% of adults had a free eye test when it was advertised only in clinics. After a national information campaign, take-up rose to 65%. The adult population is 2 million. Each test costs the state $30 and each test avoids, on average, $100 of later treatment costs. (a) Calculate the number of extra tests and their net saving to the state. (b) Explain why take-up was low before the campaign.
items.answer: (a) 500,000 extra tests; net saving $35,000,000. (b) Information failure: people underestimated the benefits of the tests or did not know about them, so the merit good was under-consumed.
items.markingKey: (a) 2m × 25% [1]; × ($100 − $30) [1] (b) information failure/merit good [2] [4]

items.stem: Why are prices of agricultural products often volatile?
options: Supply varies with the weather while demand and supply are price inelastic
items.answer: Supply varies with the weather while demand and supply are price inelastic
items.markingKey: Inelastic supply and demand + supply shocks.

items.stem: How does a buffer stock scheme stabilise prices?
options: It buys produce when prices are low and sells from stocks when prices are high
It taxes farmers in good years
It sets a fixed quantity for each farmer
items.answer: It buys produce when prices are low and sells from stocks when prices are high
items.markingKey: Floor and ceiling prices maintained by buying/selling.

items.stem: Explain how a buffer stock scheme works.
items.answer: An agency sets a minimum and maximum price. In good harvests it buys surplus output to stop the price falling below the minimum; in bad harvests it sells from stocks to stop the price rising above the maximum.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: price band; 1 mark: buy in surplus; 1 mark: sell in shortage [3]

items.stem: Demand for rice in Ostrelia is Qd = 500 − 25P (Q in thousand tonnes, P in hundreds of dollars per tonne). A buffer stock agency sets a minimum price of $1,000 per tonne (P = 10). This year’s harvest is 300 thousand tonnes. How much must the agency buy to maintain the minimum price?
items.answer: 50 thousand tonnes
items.markingKey: Qd at P = 10 is 250; harvest 300; buy 50.

items.answer: Supply shocks (weather, disease), inelastic supply and demand, time lags, cobweb behaviour, world market speculation; diagram.

items.stem: Demand for cocoa in Fendaria is Qd = 500 − 25P (Q in thousand tonnes, P in hundreds of dollars per tonne). A buffer stock agency sets a minimum price of $800 per tonne (P = 8). This year’s harvest is 320 thousand tonnes. (a) Calculate the free-market price with this harvest. (b) Calculate the quantity the agency must buy and the cost. (c) Explain one problem the agency might face if harvests are good for several years.
items.answer: (a) P = 7.2, i.e. $720 per tonne (b) 20 thousand tonnes; cost $16,000,000. (c) Stocks build up, raising storage costs and spoiling; the agency may run out of funds; it may have to lower the minimum price.

items.stem: Demand for cotton in Korvia is Qd = 400 − 20P (Q in thousand tonnes, P in hundreds of dollars per tonne). A buffer stock agency sets a minimum price of $1,200 per tonne (P = 12). (c) Explain one problem the agency might face if harvests are good for several years.

items.stem: Borealis plc produces 5,000 tonnes of chemicals a month. Its private cost is $10 per tonne, but pollution imposes an extra cost of $3 per tonne on local residents. (a) Calculate the total external cost and the total social cost each month. (b) Explain why the free market leads to over-production of the chemicals. (c) Suggest one form of intervention and explain how it would help.
items.answer: (a) External $15,000; social $65,000. (b) Borealis plc considers only private cost ($10), not the social cost ($13), so supply is too high and price too low relative to the social optimum. (c) A tax of $3 per tonne (or regulation) makes the firm pay the full social cost, reducing output towards the optimum.
items.markingKey: (a) 3 × 5000 and 13 × 5000 [2] (b) private < social cost → over-production [2] (c) policy and mechanism [1] [5]

items.stem: Sofia wrote in a homework answer: ‘Information failure only affects consumers, never producers.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: Producers can also lack information, e.g. about future prices or the true quality of inputs, and asymmetric information affects both sides.

items.stem: Explain why a good harvest can reduce farmers’ total income.
items.answer: Demand for many crops is price inelastic, so the increase in supply causes a proportionately larger fall in price, reducing total revenue.

items.stem: Extract: In Zentara, childhood vaccination rates were only 60% when parents had to pay about $30 per course. After the government made vaccinations free and ran an information campaign, the rate rose to 82%. The health ministry argues that vaccination is a merit good with large external benefits. A newspaper claims that “the market would have sorted this out on its own”. (a) Explain why vaccination is a merit good. (b) Explain the external benefits of vaccination. (c) Explain why the market alone might fail to achieve the socially optimal rate. (d) Discuss whether making vaccinations free is the best way to correct this market failure.
items.answer: (a) Parents underestimate the benefits (information failure), so it is under-consumed in a free market. (b) Vaccinated children protect others (herd immunity), lowering infection and healthcare costs for third parties. (c) Consumers ignore external benefits and underestimate private benefits; price deters low-income families. (d) Free provision raises take-up and equity vs opportunity cost, taxpayer burden, possible government failure; alternatives: information only, compulsion, subsidies; judgement.

items.stem: Why might a government want to stabilise farmers’ incomes?
options: To protect farmers from sudden falls in income and maintain food supplies
items.answer: To protect farmers from sudden falls in income and maintain food supplies
items.markingKey: Income stability, investment, food security.

items.stem: The price of coffee beans in Calvania fell by 40% after a bumper harvest. Explain why the government might intervene.
items.answer: Farmers’ incomes fall sharply, causing hardship and reducing future investment; price volatility creates uncertainty; government may buy into stocks to stabilise prices and incomes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: income/uncertainty problem; 1 mark: form of intervention [2]

items.stem: In a revision note Amara wrote: ‘A good harvest always increases farmers’ incomes because they sell more.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: If demand is price inelastic, the price falls proportionately more than quantity rises, so total income can fall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – If demand is price inelastic, the price falls proportionately more than quantity rises, so total income can fall. [2]

items.stem: Demand for cotton in Kestria is Qd = 300 − 10P (Q in thousand tonnes, P in hundreds of dollars per tonne). A buffer stock agency sets a minimum price of $1,200 per tonne (P = 12). This year’s harvest is 220 thousand tonnes. How much must the agency buy to maintain the minimum price?
items.answer: 40 thousand tonnes
items.markingKey: Qd at P = 12 is 180; harvest 220; buy 40.
